# Loop 2.0.1 on CNAPP \- installation

**Loop 2.0.1 Installation (Tailored for CNAPP instances)**

**A**

**Note:**  
This document is only applicable for the scenario of installing Loop 2.0.1 on a CNAPP VM(Both BLR and EU VMs).  
These steps are common for both BLR and EU CNAPP VMs.  
There are some additional config steps that are to be done on the Loop EU VMs, which are mentioned wherever applicable in the document below.   
This separate document is required for CNNAPP storage class constraints which require helm charts modifications.

**Background of the need of this Workaround:**

1\) When we installed Loop 2.0.1 in CNAPP VMs, the following PODs were not getting completed:  
\============  
root@srinivasamurthya-control-plane:/product/srinivasamurthya\# kubectl get pods \-n devops-loop | grep \-v Running | grep \-v Completed  
NAME                                                              READY   STATUS      RESTARTS   AGE  
devops-loop-hcl-devops-loop-learning-webserver-5c95866884-ktrt2   0/1     Pending     0          32m  
devops-loop-hcl-devopsplan-prod-0                                 0/1     Pending     0          32m  
devops-loop-hcl-devopsplan-prod-analytics-0                       0/1     Pending     0          32m  
devops-loop-hcl-devopsplan-prod-search-0                          0/1     Pending     0          32m  
devops-loop-hcl-launch-agent-prod-0                               0/1     Pending     0          32m  
devops-loop-hcl-launch-server-prod-0                              0/1     Pending     0          32m  
root@srinivasamurthya-control-plane:/product/srinivasamurthya\#   
\============

2\) The POD logs showed the error as below:  
\============  
failed to provision volume with StorageClass "standard": NodePath only supports ReadWriteOnce and ReadWriteOncePod (1.22+) access modes   
\============

3\) Reason:  
In CNAPP VMs we do not have a Storage class that supports RWX.  
We currently only have a storage class by name “standard” that supports only RWO.  
Hence the PODs that are having the RWX as a pre-requisites will fail with the above error.  
Below is the default storage class that we have on CNAPP (for reference).  
\============  
root@srinivasamurthya-control-plane:/product/srinivasamurthya\# kubectl get sc  
NAME                 PROVISIONER             RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE      ALLOWVOLUMEEXPANSION   AGE  
standard (default)   rancher.io/local-path   Delete          WaitForFirstConsumer   false                  282d  
root@srinivasamurthya-control-plane:/product/srinivasamurthya\#   
\============

**Workaround:**

We consulted one of the Dev team SPOCs of PLAN (Bahram Sanaei), who guided us to workaround this issue by forcing the failing PODs to stop looking for RWX storage and accept the RWO storage.  
*Note: This is just a workaround to install Loop 2.0.1 as of now or our CNAPP instance only and should never be shared or suggested to any customer or any one else outside this group.*

He helped us to pull the Helm chart (from the HCL Harbour repo) of the Loop 2.0.1 locally onto the VM local path to a directory.  
Identified the charts of each of the above PODs that are failing, found the lines that are pointing to “RWX” storage and replaced it with “RWO”. 

Then in the helm install command, instead of pointing to HCL harbour repo, we pointed to the local repo directory that has the modified charts. Which helped in installing the Loop 2.0.1 forcefully with only RWO and over ruling the need of RWX storage class.

This is just a workaround for the current Loop version 2.0.1 and it is not feasible to replicate this step of identifying the files and manually editing the charts every time.  
Hence the plan for now is: we have created a tar of the whole directory of this Local repo and uploaded in the Loop google space in below path: [2.0.1-hcl-local-repo.tar](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1kfuI13phYbEQtFUuezUx5Xsz0t7gvWH5/view?usp=drive_link)

So the expectation is that, any TSE from our group who is trying to install Loop 2.0.1 on CNAPP VM, can download this tar file to the VM they are working on and proceed with the Loop 2.0.1 installation by pointing to it.

**Prerequisites to verify before installing Loop:**

**1\) Helm version.**  
Verify the Helm version before performing the Loop installation.   
Because in some CNAPP VMs it was seen the helm version was 3.6.3.  
But Loop needs Helm 3.17 and above.  
So first upgrade the Helm version to the latest version   
(Example 3.19.2 is one of the versions that we have seen is working on CNAPP VMs without any issue with Loop installation)  
Helm 3.19.2 bits are placed on our Loop space in the path here \-\> [Helm-3.19.2](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1yZTZ38p94n3SVSRmHkv0VfoY9DFRt0SJ/view?usp=drive_link)  
(You can get the latest Helm version from the link: [https://github.com/helm/helm/releases](https://github.com/helm/helm/releases) )  
Then do the below steps for upgrade the Helm version: (Reference: [https://helm.sh/docs/intro/install/](https://helm.sh/docs/intro/install/) )  
\=============  
1\) Download the helm installer bits to your VM.

2\) Unpack it (Example: gunzip [helm-v4.0.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz](http://helm-v4.0.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz), followed by  tar \-xvf [helm-v4.0.0-linux-amd64.tar](http://helm-v4.0.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz))  
3\) Run the command to replace the helm executable with the latest helm version \-\>  “mv linux-amd64/helm /usr/local/bin/helm”  
This completes the helm upgrade

Verify helm version as below, it should now show the upgraded Helm version:  
root@srinivasamurthya-control-plane:/loop-install/scripts\# **helm version**  
version.BuildInfo{Version:**"v3.19.2"**, GitCommit:"8766e718a0119851f10ddbe4577593a45fadf544", GitTreeState:"clean", GoVersion:"go1.24.9"}  
root@srinivasamurthya-control-plane:/loop-install/scripts\#  
\=============

**The steps to be performed for installing the Loop 2.0.1 are as below:**

1\) Download the [2.0.1-hcl-local-repo.tar](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1kfuI13phYbEQtFUuezUx5Xsz0t7gvWH5/view?usp=drive_link) to your CNAPP VM.

2\) Untar it and make sure it has following files:  
root@srinivasamurthya-control-plane:/loop-install/scripts/win-copy\# ls \-ltr 2.0.1-hcl-local-repo  
total 24  
\-rwxrwxrwx 1 root root  418 May  1 10:27 secrets.sh  
drwxr-xr-x 8 root root 4096 May  4 15:12 hcl-devops-loop  
\-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  369 May 11 08:04 emissary-ports.yaml  
\-rwxrwxrwx 1 root root 1054 May 11 08:08 prereq.sh  
\-rwxr-xr-x 1 root root 6708 May 14 02:44 loop-2.0.1-install-localrepo.sh  
root@srinivasamurthya-control-plane:/loop-install/scripts/win-copy\#

3\) You have to edit the following points to match your specific CNAPP VM (cluster name and IP address)

a) In secrets.sh update your cluster name instead of my VMs cluster name:

You can run below command to identify your cluster name first:  
\===========  
root@srinivasamurthya-control-plane:/product/srinivasamurthya/loop/loop\_201/upload\# kubectl config get-clusters  
NAME  
**srinivasamurthya**  
root@srinivasamurthya-control-plane:/product/srinivasamurthya/loop/loop\_201/upload\#  
\===========

Then edit the below line in secrets.sh to update the cluster name, replace “srinivasamurthya” with the cluster name that you identify from above command.  
\===========  
kubectl config set-context devops-loop \--namespace=devops-loop \--cluster=**srinivasamurthya** \--user=kubernetes-admin  
\===========

b) For installing on EU CNAPP only, you perform the steps mentioned here in point \#b and then proceed to \#c & \#d.  
If its not EU CNAPP you can skip \#b and go to step \#c.

in prereq.sh script, edit the below line to add the actual IP address of your EU VM instance/host.  
\========  
kubectl patch service emissary-ingress \-n emissary \-p "{\\"spec\\": {\\"externalIPs\\": **\[\\"$(hostname \-I | awk '{print $1}')\\"\]**}}"   
\========

The line should look like below after edit, in place of IP “10.14.43.176”, you should have mentioned your EU VM instance or host IP:  
\========  
kubectl patch service emissary-ingress \-n emissary \-p '{"spec": {"externalIPs": **\["10.14.43.176"\]**}}'     // IPAddress of the VM  
\========

c) in loop-2.0.1-install-localrepo.sh: replace the Ingress IP with your VM IP in the line:   
(replace “10.14.43.179” with the IP of your VM instance)   
INGRESS\_IP=**10.14.43.179**

d) The loop install script loop-2.0.1-install-localrepo.sh, is already edited to point to the local repo where you have untarred the folder. 

So you can proceed with the Loop 2.0.1 installation. It will pick the edited charts from the local directory “hcl-devops-loop” (the line shown below) and it won't try to pull the charts from HCL Harbor.  
Below is the line in the script, where it is pointing to the local repo path for the edited charts.  
\============  
 helm upgrade \--install ${HELM\_NAME} **./hcl-devops-loop** ${HELM\_OPTIONS} \\  
    \-n ${NAMESPACE} \--timeout=10m0s || return 1 \#--dry-run=server   /loop-install/scripts/debugInstallLog.txt    
\============

e) You can run the scripts in this order after you have edited as per the above mentioned points:  
\======  
1\) ./prereq.sh  
2\) ./secrets.sh  
3\) ./loop-2.0.1-install-localrepo.sh   
\======

**Note:** Sometimes you might face an error like below when you execute Loop install script.  
Just re-run the Loop install script again and it should go through like shown below:

root@srinivasamurthya-control-plane:/loop-install/scripts/2.0.1-hcl\# ./loop-2.0.1-instal-localrepo.sh

# Loop Doc Thoughts

Order of the actions:  
We need to be clear in which order steps need to be taken where.  
This Guide first had the ‘Control’ section above the ‘Build’ section.  
But if you push an artifact to the Control repository it will automatically trigger a Build in Build.  
As you have not configured Build yet, this will cause the build to fail.

(I think it is likely that the sections of this document were just added randomly, whenever the product team was done with it.  
Not based on actual usage of Loop.)

Screenshots:  
Screenshots should be full screen screenshots, so that you do not have to guess where in the webUI you are

Text in screenshots should also be in plain text.  
Examples in screenshots are nice, but you cannot copy paste it.  
Unless you specifically want the reader to have to manually type it, also document what you show in screenshots in text.

# Plan Doc Thoughts

# Build – Configurations on Loop

### **📘 DevOps Build** 

**This guide details the IBM DevOps Build process within the Loop environment, explaining how source code is transformed into deployable artifacts, how to configure the build system, and how to troubleshoot common issues.**

---

### **1\. Overview & Purpose**

**What is Build? In the DevOps process, "Build" is the critical bridge between development and deployment. Its primary objective is to transform source code into a deployable artifact (e.g., a .war file) through automation.**

**Key Objectives:**

* **Compile & Validate: Ensure code compiles correctly.**  
* **Package: Create the application package (e.g., .war).**  
* **Store: Save the artifact immutably in CodeStation.**  
* **Traceability: Link the artifact version directly back to the specific Commit ID.**

---

### **2\. The Build Flow**

**The automated flow moves from the repository trigger to artifact storage:**

1. **Repository (IBM Loop Control): A merge to the main branch triggers the process.**  
2. **DevOps Build Server: Receives the trigger and assigns a job to an available agent.**  
3. **DevOps Build Agent: Executes the steps defined in the Process Template (Pull source → Compile → Package).**  
4. **CodeStation: The final artifact is published and stored here, ready for the Deployment pipeline.**

---

### **3\. Core Components**

| Component | Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Repository** | **Git-based storage in IBM Loop Control. Commits here trigger the build.** |
| **Build Server** | **Orchestrates jobs, manages agents, and maintains build history/logs.** |
| **Build Agent** | **The "worker" that executes the shell scripts and compiles the code.** |
| **CodeStation** | **The built-in artifact repository that ensures versioned, immutable storage.** |

---

### **4\. Hands-on Configuration Steps**

**To set up a build, practitioners must configure Agents, Templates, and Jobs within the Loop interface.**

#### **Step i: Accessing Build**

**Navigate to the Build solution from the Loop menu.**

![][image27]

* **Configuration:**

  * **Set the Maximum Number of Jobs (e.g., 5).**  
  * **Assign it to Agent Pools (e.g., "All Build Agents").**  
  * **Save**

 **Ensure the status turns Green (Configured/Online)**![][image29]

**Templates define the project.**

* **Create Template: Under Templates, create a new project(e.g., Project-DemoLoop\~DevOps).**

![][image30]

**Step iv: Creating Process Templates – defines the build workflow, including compilation, testing, and artifact generation.**  
**Templates define the workflow.**

* **Create Template: Under Templates, create a new process (e.g., Process-DemoLoop\~DevOps).**  
*  **Under Definition: Add job to the visual workflow designer:**

![][image31]

**Step v: Creating Source Templates – defines how and where to fetch the source code (Git, Bitbucket, control etc.).**  
**Templates define the workflow.**

* **Create Template: Under Templates, create a new source(e.g., Source-DemoLoop\~DevOps).**

![][image32]

#### **Step vi: Creating Job/Step Template – defines the detailed commands or scripts that run in each step of the build.**

**Templates define the workflow.**

* **Create Template: Under Templates, create a new Jobs(e.g., Job-DemoLoop\~DevOps).**  
* **Define Steps: Add steps to the visual workflow designer:**

**Step-by-Step Breakdown**

* **1\. Creating Stamp:	Create Stamp	Generates a unique build identifier (like Build\_2025\_11\_03\_01)	Used for naming versions and tracking builds**  
  * **2\. Disable Control SSL:	Shell Script	Runs a shell command to disable SSL checks or set environment flags	Useful if your build server connects to internal control with self-signed certs**  
  * **3\. Cleaning Workspace:	Clean Workspace	Deletes previous build outputs	Ensures clean environment before new build**  
  * **4\. Populating Workspace:	Populate Workspace	Pulls the latest source code from repository	Downloads repo code from GitHub/GitLab based on the trigger**  
  * **5\. Get Change Logs:	Get Source Changes	Fetches commit history since last build	Used for tracking what changed and triggering conditional builds**  
  * **6\. Build the Artifacts: we’re executing a simple shell script to compile and package our source files into a deployable artifact**   
  * **7\. Upload Artifacts to CodeStation	CodeStation \- Upload All Artifacts	Uploads the generated build output to CodeStation	Stores build outputs as versioned artifacts (immutable)**  
  * **8\. Creating Component Version in Deploy for APP	DevOps Deploy Integration	Creates a new version in UrbanCode Deploy for APP component	Makes build artifact available for deployment**  
  * **9\. Creating Component Version in Deploy for WEB	DevOps Deploy Integration	Same as above for the web tier component	Enables deployment of web service**  
  * **10\. Creating Component Version in Deploy for DB	DevOps Deploy Integration	Same for database component	Keeps all layers in sync with this build**  
  * **11\. Creating Snapshot in Deploy	DevOps Deploy Integration	Combines APP \+ WEB \+ DB component versions into one snapshot	Snapshot \= consistent set of component versions for one deployment**  
  * **12\. Deploying Snapshot	DevOps Deploy Integration	Deploys the created snapshot to the target environment	Runs the actual deployment process in UCD**  
  * **13\. Waiting for Deployment	Shell Script	Waits for deployment status (polling UCD API or logs)	Ensures job doesn’t finish before deploy completes**  
  * **14\. Assigning Success	Assign Status	Marks build as SUCCESS if all prior steps passed	Used for job reporting and triggers**  
  * **15\. Assigning Failure	Assign Status	Marks build as FAILED if any step fails	Used for error tracking and alerts**

![][image33]  
 **Step vii:Build the Artifacts: we’re executing a simple shell script to compile and package our source files into a deployable artifact — in this case, a WAR file for the JPetStore application.**   
**Once built, we place it inside the app/ folder so that the next step, Upload Artifacts to CodeStation, can automatically detect and upload it.**   
**This ensures the build artifacts are versioned and traceable within our DevOps pipeline.”  This step creates the deployable file JPetStore.war.**   
**The next step (Upload Artifacts to CodeStation) picks up the contents from the workspace — specifically app/JPetStore.war.**   
**CodeStation stores that artifact with a version number (e.g., 1.0.12). Later steps (Create Component Version In Deploy) link that version to UrbanCode Deploy components.**

Script :-  
*echo "=== Cleaning and preparing build workspace \==="*  
*rm \-rf app && mkdir app*  
*echo "=== Packaging JPetStore application \==="*  
*jar cvf JPetStore.war META-INF WEB-INF account cart catalog common help.html images index.html order*  
*echo "=== Moving WAR to app directory \==="*  
*cp JPetStore.war app/*  
*echo "=== Build complete: app/JPetStore.war created \==="*  
*ls \-lh app/*

![][image34]

**Include patterns : Use the Artifacts DB created from step build the artifact and uploaded Artifacts to CodeStation.**

![][image38]

**Repository Trigger: We integrate directly with source control so the build can be triggered automatically based on events — like a new commit, a pull request, or a merge.**  
**This ensures continuous integration — meaning code is built and validated immediately after every change. enabled the repository trigger — so the build starts automatically when developers push code to the any branch**  
![][image41]

**Project Trigger: These are custom triggers you can customize to specific projects instead of the whole repository integrated, the source control so the build can be triggered automatically based on events — like a new commit, a pull request, or a merge.**  
**This ensures continuous integration — meaning code is built and validated immediately after every change. enabled the project trigger**

---

### **5\. Execution & Verification**

**Execution Triggers:**

* **Automatic: Triggered by a webhook on a "merge to main" event.**  
* **Manual: You can manually request a build via the "Request Build" button in the interface.**

**Verification Checklist:**

**Once the build completes, verify the following:**

1. **✅ Status: Build status shows "Success".**  
2. **✅ Artifacts: The .war file is present in CodeStation.**  
3. **✅ Traceability: The version maps correctly to the Commit ID.**  
4. **✅ Logs: Build logs are generated and accessible.**

---

### **6\. Troubleshooting & Best Practices**

#### **Troubleshooting Common Issues**

| Issue | Likely Cause | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Build not triggered** | **Merge rule missing** | **Validate the repository webhook.** |
| **Agent offline** | **Service down** | **Restart the build agent service.** |
| **Artifact missing** | **Publish step failed** | **Check the shell script logic in the template.** |
| **Wrong version** | **Branch mismatch** | **Verify the source branch configuration.** |

#### **Best Practices**

* **Immutable Artifacts: Never overwrite an existing artifact version.**  
* **Merge-Based Triggers: Rely on merge events rather than direct commits for stability.**  
* **Single Build: Do not rebuild for higher environments (e.g., QA/Prod); promote the *existing* artifact.**  
* **Traceability: Always maintain the mapping between the Commit ID and the Artifact.**

# Deploy \- Confiiguration on Loop

# DevOps Deploy

1. ### **Overview** & **Purpose** :

          **What is DevOps Deploy?** DevOps Deploy is an enterprise deployment solution. Use DevOps Deploy (Deploy) to standardize and simplify the process of deploying software components to each environment in your development cycle. It emphasizes collaboration between development and operations teams, aiming to accelerate software delivery and improve application quality.

2. ### **Core Functionality of Deploy**

* **Release Automation**: Automates the entire release process, reducing manual errors and accelerating deployments.  
* **Visibility and Traceability**: Provides comprehensive insights into application versions, environments, and configurations, ensuring compliance and auditing capabilities.  
* **Environment Modeling**: Define and manage complete application topology across multiple deployment environments.  
* **Integrations**: Offers integrations with various tools like Jenkins, Kubernetes, Microsoft, ServiceNow, and IBM WebSphere, enhancing process robustness.

### **3\. Deploy Architecture**

* **Deploy Server**: Central hub, workflow engine, User interface, Maintain history and audit trails  
* **Agents**: Lightweight processes on target systems  
* **Repositories**: Artifacts storage  
  **Database**: Configuration and Deployment history


### **4\. Key Elements**

| Elements | Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| Applications | The overall container for your software, defining environments and processes. |
| Environments |  Logical destinations (e.g., Dev, Test, Prod) where applications are deployed, mapping to target servers. |
| Components |  Group related deployable artifacts (code, config files) and their versions.  |
| Processes | Graphical workflows (steps like install, configure, test) that automate deployment actions on components within environments. |
| Resources & Agents | Target machines (Resources) where agents are installed to execute process steps |
| Snapshots |  Collections of specific component versions known to work together, used for consistent deployments |

Additional Resources

* Elements overview: [IBM Docs \- Elements Overview](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/devops-deploy/8.2.0?topic=deploy-elements-overview)  
* Firewall and communication setup: [IBM Docs \- Firewall Configuration](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/devops-deploy/8.2.0?topic=installing-firewall-communication-configuration)

### **5\. Hands-on Configuration Steps**

Click the “Deploy” icon in the Solutions list, as shown below. This will open “Deploy” in a new browser tab:

#### **5.1: Configure Deploy Service for External Communication**

Overview

This guide details the steps required to configure the containerized Deploy server to accept connections from external (on-premise) agents. This involves exposing the Kubernetes service via a LoadBalancer with a static External IP and ensuring the necessary communication ports are open on the Emissary ingress.

Add External IP

1. **Determine your Kubernetes Host IP:** Use ifconfig (Linux/Mac) or ipconfig (Windows) to find the IP address of your Kubernetes host node. (Example used below: 10.190.116.49).  
2. **Identify the Kubernetes Service:** List the services to confirm the correct service name.  
*  Run \`kubectl get svc\` to list services.  
*  Identify the \`devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod\` or ‘**devops-loop-hcl-launch-server-prod’**  service.

     Note:

  IBM Service: **devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod**

  HCL Service: **devops-loop-hcl-launch-server-prod**


3.  Edit the Service Type:   
*      Edit the service using \`kubectl edit svc devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod\`.  
*      Change the service type from \`type: ClusterIP\` to \`type: LoadBalancer\`


4. Patching the Service to add External IP:  
   Run the patch command to append the externalIPs field to the service specification. Replace the IP address below with your actual Host IP.

                  $ **kubectl patch service devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod \-p '{"spec": {"externalIPs": \["10.190.116.49"\]}}'**

   

5. Verification: Confirm that the External IP and TYPE have been successfully applied.

   $ **kubectl get svc devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod \-o wide**

   NAME                       TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP     PORT(S)                         AGE   SELECTOR

   devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod   **LoadBalancer**   10.96.96.160   **10.190.116.49**   8080:30635/TCP,7919:31531/TCP   42d   [app.kubernetes.io/component=srv,app.kubernetes.io/instance=devops-loop,app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-ucd-prod](http://app.kubernetes.io/component=srv,app.kubernetes.io/instance=devops-loop,app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-ucd-prod)

Expected Outpu**t:** The EXTERNAL-IP column should now display your host IP (e.g., 10.190.116.49) instead of \<none\>. You can now connect your external DB client using this IP and Port 3306\.

**DevOps-component-JPetStore-APP component**

This screenshot shows the Process Design for the **`DevOps-component-JPetStore-APP`**.  
The flow follows a standard linear deployment pattern:

**Deployment Workflow Steps**

1. **Clean working directory:** Deletes existing files and directories to ensure a "fresh" environment.  
2. **Download Artifacts:** Pulls the specific version of the application code/binaries from the repository.  
3. **Unzip:** Extracts the downloaded files.  Update the value as app/JPetStore.war  
4. **Update property file:** Modifies Java Properties files, likely injected with environment-specific variables (like DB connections).  
5. **Create .zip File:** Re-packages the updated files, potentially for archiving or final placement.  
6. **Start Tomcat:** Ensures the application server is running.  
7. **Undeploy Application:** Removes any previous version of the app currently running on the server.  
8. **Deploy Application:** Installs the new version to the server.

![][image56]

**DevOps-component-JPetStore-DB component**

This screenshot shows the Process Design for the **`DevOps-component-JPetStore-DB`**.  
This process focuses on Database Schema updates

* **Download Artifacts:** Pulls the database scripts or migration files  
* **Upgrade DB:** Executes the SQL scripts or migration commands to bring the database schema up to date with the application version. Update the DB Driver Jar field as db/1.0/lib/\<connector-jar\>

![][image57]

**DevOps-component-JPetStore-WEB component**

This screenshot shows the Process Design for the **`DevOps-component-JPetStore-WEB`.**

* **Clean working directory:** Uses the "Delete Files and Directories" step to ensure no stale data remains.  
* **Download Artifacts:** Pulls the latest web content.  
* **Remove old content:** A secondary deletion step to target specific old directories before the new move.  
* **Deploy new content:** Uses the "Move Directory" step to place the new web assets in their final destination.

# Measure \- Configuration on Loop

# **DevOps Measure**

1. ### **Overview & Purpose :**

Velocity automates processes in your release lifecycle and gathers insights into your DevOps processes. It is an enterprise-scale release management service that supports both cloud-native and on-premises deployment tools. For more information about the Velocity, see [Overview of DevOps Velocity](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/SSCKX6_5.2.x/user/topics/c_overview_se.html).

2. ### **Key elements:**

| Elements | Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| Value Streams | A value stream represents the objects and activities that you employ to deliver customer value, from initial concept to final delivered project.The value stream provides a strategic window into your project workflow and enables you to drill-down to individual objects. The objects, such as builds, pull requests, issues, and tests, come from tools that you integrate into the value stream. Individual objects are represented graphically by small circles called dots. Dots frequently provide information from logically related tools, such as issues linked to source control commits. |
| Pipelines | Pipelines provide a streamlined method to manage the applications in your development lifecycle. With pipelines, you can auto-generate deployment plans and deploy applications versions to all environments. |
| Dots | Graphical representations of individual work items (e.g., builds, pull requests, Jira issues, or commits) that move through the value stream. |
| Integrations (Plugins) | Connections to external tools like Jenkins, Jira, GitHub, SonarQube, and ServiceNow to aggregate data into a single view. |
| Insights (Metrics) | A data-driven dashboard providing DevOps metrics (like metrics, cycle time, and lead time) to assess project efficiency and quality. |

3. ### **Hands-on Configuration Steps**

   Click the “Measure” icon in the Solutions list, as shown below. This will open “Measure” in a new browser tab:

![][image65]

**Measure** dashboard, shows a **Value Stream** management view. 

![][image66]

When you create a new Loop, the system provisions these distinct integration types to pull data from various stages of your delivery pipeline.

To ensure your data remains current, keep an eye on the **Status** and **Last sync** columns in your settings. Here is a quick guide on how the synchronization works:

* **Normal Operation**: All active integrations should display an **"Online"** status.  
* **Automatic Syncing**: The system is configured to perform a background sync every **5 minutes** by default.  
* **Manual Refresh**: If you need to trigger an immediate data update, you can toggle the **"Disable/Enable"** switch to force a resync.

4. ### **Breakdown of Automated Integrations**

These integrations feed the Value Stream metrics you saw earlier:

* **IBM DevOps Deploy (DeployLoops):** This connects to your deployment engine to track when code actually hits environments.  
* **DevOps Build:** Tracks CI (Continuous Integration) activity, providing data on build frequency and success rates.  
* **DevOps Control:** Likely manages the orchestration or gating data between different stages of the Loop.  
* **DevOps Plan:** Syncs with your planning tools.  
* **DevOps Test Hub:** Pulls in quality metrics and test results.

![][image67]

5. ### **Value Stream Overview**

When you create a new Loop, the system provisions these distinct integration types to pull data from various stages of your delivery pipeline.

The value stream visualizes the end-to-end flow of work items—such as **Tasks**, **Stories**, and **Defects**—from submission to deployment in the **DEV** environment.

**Stages of the Pipeline**

Work moves through the following stages as captured by your integrations:

* **Submitted:** New requests entering the system.  **"query": "issue.status \= \\"Submitted\\"".**  
* **Backlog :** Work prioritized and ready for development. **"query": "issue.status \= \\"Backlog\\"".**  
* **In Progress :** Active development work. **"query": "issue.status \= \\"Active\\"".**  
* **In Review:**  Under code review. **"query": "issue.status \= \\"Resolved\\" AND (pr.status \= \\"open\\" OR pr.status \= \\"review\\")"**.  
* **Completed:** Work that has finished the development/review phase.   
  **"query": "issue.status \= \\"Closed\\" AND (pr.status \= \\"merged\\" OR pr.status \= \\"closed\\") AND (deployment.env \!= \\"DEVOPS-DEV-ENV\\" AND deployment.env \!= \\"DEVOPS-QA-ENV\\" AND deployment.env \!= \\"DEVOPS-PROD-ENV\\") AND (build.status \!= \\"Failure\\" AND build.status \!= \\"success\\")"**  
* **Build Stages:**  
  * **Failed Build:** Shows Failed Build.  
     **"query": "issue.status \= \\"Closed\\" AND build.status \= \\"Failure\\" AND (deployment.env \!= \\"DEVOPS-DEV-ENV\\" AND deployment.env \!= \\"DEVOPS-QA-ENV\\" AND deployment.env \!= \\"DEVOPS-PROD-ENV\\")"**  
  * **Success Build:**   
     **"query": "issue.status \= \\"Closed\\" AND build.status \= \\"success\\" AND (deployment.env \!= \\"DEVOPS-DEV-ENV\\" AND deployment.env\!= \\"DEVOPS-QA-ENV\\" AND deployment.env\!= \\"DEVOPS-PROD-ENV\\")"**  
* **DEV :** The final stage of automation by loop, representing items deployed to the development environment.  
  **"query": "deployment.env \= \\"DEVOPS-DEV-ENV\\" AND deployment.env \!= \\"DEVOPS-QA-ENV\\" AND deployment.env \!= \\"DEVOPS-PROD-ENV\\""**  
  **QA:** Versions which are deployed on QA environment   
            **"query": "deployment.env \= \\"DEVOPS-QA-ENV\\" AND deployment.env \!= \\"DEVOPS-PROD-ENV\\""**  
* **PROD:** Versions which are deployed on PROD environment  
            **"query": "deployment.env \= \\"DEVOPS-PROD-ENV\\""**

# **IBM DevOps Loop Practitioner Guide / Hands-on User Guide**

# **Introduction**

This guide provides a hands-on walkthrough for practitioners on how to use DevOps Loop for a CI-CD (Continuous Integration & Continuous Deployment) implementation.  
In this demonstration we will be using DevOps Loop for making a change in the JpetStore App \- where we try to add a new Dog category called “Bichon”.  
While doing this, we will see how CI-CD methodology can be implemented in Loop \- starting from entering a Workitem in Plan to visualising the deployment changes moving to various stages on the Measure Value stream.

# **Prerequisites:**  1\) This document assumes that the practitioner reviewing this guide has already installed Loop, created required TeamSpace and the Loop

2\) Have deployed the initial code of the JpetStore App using the below steps:  
\<include link of hosting JpetStore App on Deploy) 

# **Steps in DevOps Plan**

After creating the Loop, the first thing is to start with the creation of a new record in Plan (or modifying an existing record) for tracking the source code changes and associating these changes with the record.  
The following steps are performed in the DevOps Plan (e.g., for Loop "**DevOp**").

1) Click on the “Plan” icon from the list of Solutions, as shown below. This will open “Plan” in a new browser tab:  
     
   ![][image72]  
 


2) You can see that a new application with the name “DevOp” is available, as highlighted. Note that the Plan application picks up the first 5 characters from the Loop name for its application name.   
   We can enter into this application by clicking on “Lets go” as shown below.   
     
   ![][image73]  
     
     
3) Now we have to create a new Workitem to capture the details of the change that is needed to be done. In our current example, we will create a workitem to add the new Dog category called “Bichon” in the JpetStore app.

   Click on the drop down menu from the right hand top corner as shown below and select the “Workitem” option:

   ![][image74]  
     
4) A new Workitem record form will open as shown below. We will fill the required fields like Title, Project, Owner, etc in the form. And finally submit the Workitem by clicking on “Save”.  
     
   ![][image75]  
     
5) Once the record is saved, we can see that it will have a unique ID as shown below.   
   Ex: “DevOp00000045” is created as shown below, and it will initially remain in the Submitted state.  
     
   ![][image76]  
     
     
6) We need to change the state of this record from Submitted to Backlog to start the lifecycle of continuous integration (CI). To do this, click on “Change State” drop down at the right top corner and select “Backlog” and save it:  
   ![][image77]  
     
7) Once the changes are saved, the state of the record is changed to “Backlog” as seen below:  
   ![][image78]  
     
8) Once the Workitem “DevOp00000045” is transitioned to the Backlog state, we can see the same in the Measure Value Stream. For doing this, we will select the “Measure” solution from the list as shown below.  
     
   ![][image79]  
     
9) In the Value stream, if we hover mouse over the dot, we can see the pop up showing the record ID “DevOp00000045” in the “Submitted” column.  
   ![][image80]  
     
     
10) To continue with the CI, we need to make sure the work item is assigned to an owner and the state of the record is changed from “Backlog” to “Active”. To change the state, click on “Change state” drop down again and click on “Start” as shown below:  
    ![][image81]  
      
      
    Once the record is saved, the state will be shown as “Active” on the record, as seen below:

    ![][image83]  
      
11) This completes the prerequisites from the Plan perspective. We will next go to the “Control” solution for making the source code changes for implementing this change.

# **📘 DevOps Build** 

**This guide details the IBM DevOps Build process within the Loop environment, explaining how source code is transformed into deployable artifacts, how to configure the build system, and how to troubleshoot common issues.**

**1\. Overview & Purpose :**  
**What is Build? In the DevOps process, "Build" is the critical bridge between development and deployment. Its primary objective is to transform source code into a deployable artifact (e.g., a .war file) through automation.**

**As soon as new code is committed to source control, the build is automatically triggered. Each build has inputs, storage, and outputs: We can see that in the Build the Artifacts step.**   
**Inputs: Source code, build scripts, configuration files, and environment variables.**  
**Storage: CodeStation (CodeStation is internal artifact repository).**  
**Output: are the generated artifacts the code is manifated into its deployable format— for example, java application as .jar, Web application as .war, Enterprise application as .ear and many more formats.zip, or Docker image.”After the build finishes, the generated artifact is automatically uploaded and becomes available for the Deploy stage.**

**Key Objectives:**

* **Compile & Validate: Ensure code compiles correctly.**  
* **Package: Create the application package (e.g., .war).**  
* **Store: Save the artifact immutably in CodeStation.**  
* **Traceability: Link the artifact version directly back to the specific Commit ID.**

### **2\. The Build Flow**

**The automated flow moves from the repository trigger to artifact storage:**

* **Repository (IBM Loop Control): A merge to the main branch triggers the process.**  
* **DevOps Build Server: Receives the trigger and assigns a job to an available agent.**  
* **DevOps Build Agent: Executes the steps defined in the Process Template (Pull source → Compile → Package).**  
* **CodeStation: The final artifact is published and stored here, ready for the Deployment pipeline.**

### **3\. Core Components**

| Component | Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Repository** | **Git-based storage in IBM Loop Control. Commits here trigger the build.** |
| **Build Server** | **Orchestrates jobs, manages agents, and maintains build history/logs.** |
| **Build Agent** | **The "worker" that executes the shell scripts and compiles the code.** |
| **CodeStation** | **The built-in artifact repository that ensures versioned, immutable storage.** |

### **4\. Hands-on Configuration Steps**

**To set up a build, practitioners must configure Agents, Templates, and Jobs within the Loop interface.**

#### **Step i: Accessing Build**

**Navigate to the Build solution from the Loop menu.**

![][image103]

#### **Step ii: Configuring Agents**

**Agents execute the actual work. You must ensure they are online and configured correctly.**

* **Navigate: Go to the Agents tab.**

**Step-by-Step Breakdown**

* **1\. Creating Stamp:	Create Stamp	Generates a unique build identifier (like Build\_2025\_11\_03\_01)	Used for naming versions and tracking builds**  
  * **2\. Disable Control SSL:	Shell Script	Runs a shell command to disable SSL checks or set environment flags	Useful if your build server connects to internal control with self-signed certs**  
  * **3\. Cleaning Workspace:	Clean Workspace	Deletes previous build outputs	Ensures clean environment before new build**  
  * **4\. Populating Workspace:	Populate Workspace	Pulls the latest source code from repository	Downloads repo code from GitHub/GitLab based on the trigger**  
  * **5\. Get Change Logs:	Get Source Changes	Fetches commit history since last build	Used for tracking what changed and triggering conditional builds**  
  * **6\. Build the Artifacts: we’re executing a simple shell script to compile and package our source files into a deployable artifact**   
  * **7\. Upload Artifacts to CodeStation	CodeStation \- Upload All Artifacts	Uploads the generated build output to CodeStation	Stores build outputs as versioned artifacts (immutable)**  
  * **8\. Creating Component Version in Deploy for APP	DevOps Deploy Integration	Creates a new version in UrbanCode Deploy for APP component	Makes build artifact available for deployment**  
  * **9\. Creating Component Version in Deploy for WEB	DevOps Deploy Integration	Same as above for the web tier component	Enables deployment of web service**  
  * **10\. Creating Component Version in Deploy for DB	DevOps Deploy Integration	Same for database component	Keeps all layers in sync with this build**  
  * **11\. Creating Snapshot in Deploy	DevOps Deploy Integration	Combines APP \+ WEB \+ DB component versions into one snapshot	Snapshot \= consistent set of component versions for one deployment**  
  * **12\. Deploying Snapshot	DevOps Deploy Integration	Deploys the created snapshot to the target environment	Runs the actual deployment process in UCD**  
  * **13\. Waiting for Deployment	Shell Script	Waits for deployment status (polling UCD API or logs)	Ensures job doesn’t finish before deploy completes**  
  * **14\. Assigning Success	Assign Status	Marks build as SUCCESS if all prior steps passed	Used for job reporting and triggers**  
  * **15\. Assigning Failure	Assign Status	Marks build as FAILED if any step fails	Used for error tracking and alerts**

# **Steps in DevOps Deploy**

# **Part 1: Configure Deploy Service for External Communication**

**Overview**

This guide details the steps required to configure the containerized Deploy server to accept connections from external (on-premise) agents. This involves exposing the Kubernetes service via a LoadBalancer with a static External IP and ensuring the necessary communication ports are open on the Emissary ingress.

# **Add External IP**

1. **Determine your Kubernetes Host IP:** Use ifconfig (Linux/Mac) or ipconfig (Windows) to find the IP address of your Kubernetes host node. (Example used below: 10.190.116.49).  
2. **Identify the Kubernetes Service:** List the services to confirm the correct service name.  
*  Run \`kubectl get svc\` to list services.  
*  Identify the \`devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod\` or ‘**devops-loop-hcl-launch-server-prod’**  service.

     Note:

  IBM Service: **devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod**

  HCL Service: **devops-loop-hcl-launch-server-prod**


3.  Edit the Service Type:   
*      Edit the service using \`kubectl edit svc devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod\`.  
*      Change the service type from \`type: ClusterIP\` to \`type: LoadBalancer\`


4. Patching the Service to add External IP:  
   Run the patch command to append the externalIPs field to the service specification. Replace the IP address below with your actual Host IP.

                  $ **kubectl patch service devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod \-p '{"spec": {"externalIPs": \["10.190.116.49"\]}}'**

   

5. Verification: Confirm that the External IP and TYPE have been successfully applied.

   $ **kubectl get svc devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod \-o wide**

   NAME                       TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP     PORT(S)                         AGE   SELECTOR

   devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod   **LoadBalancer**   10.96.96.160   **10.190.116.49**   8080:30635/TCP,7919:31531/TCP   42d   [app.kubernetes.io/component=srv,app.kubernetes.io/instance=devops-loop,app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-ucd-prod](http://app.kubernetes.io/component=srv,app.kubernetes.io/instance=devops-loop,app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-ucd-prod)

**Expected Output:** The EXTERNAL-IP column should now display your host IP (e.g., 10.190.116.49) instead of \<none\>. You can now connect your external DB client using this IP and Port 3306\.

### **Deployment Workflow Steps**

1. **Clean working directory:** Deletes existing files and directories to ensure a "fresh" environment.  
2. **Download Artifacts:** Pulls the specific version of the application code/binaries from the repository.  
3. **Unzip:** Extracts the downloaded files.  
4. **Update property file:** Modifies Java Properties files, likely injected with environment-specific variables (like DB connections).  
5. **Create .zip File:** Re-packages the updated files, potentially for archiving or final placement.  
6. **Start Tomcat:** Ensures the application server is running.  
7. **Undeploy Application:** Removes any previous version of the app currently running on the server.  
8. **Deploy Application:** Installs the new version to the server.

# **Configure Deploy Service for External Agent Communication**

To allow external (on-premise) agents to communicate with the containerized Deploy server, the K8S service must be exposed via a LoadBalancer with a static External IP.

1. **Determine Kubernetes Host IP:** Use `ifconfig` or `ipconfig` (Example: 10.190.116.49).

# **TroubleShooting**

# **Check External IP and Ports are Enabled on Pods**

# 1How to Check External IP and Ports are Enabled on Pods

**1\. Test from the same host where Kubernetes is installed**

* **Command:** `telnet <host IP> port`  
* **Action:** If the connection is not successful, Patch the Emissary Ports.

**2\. Test from an external agent on a different host or connect to the database from a client outside**

* **Step A:** `ping Host_IP`  
  * **Action:** If the initial attempt is unsuccessful, collaborate with the firewall team to establish connectivity.  
* **Step B:** Run the telnet command  
  * **Command:** `telnet <host IP> port`  
  * **Action:** If it is not connected successfully:  
    * b.1. Check Patch Emissary Ports.  
    * b.2. Work with the firewall team to open ports.

# **Resolving HTTP 413 "Request Entity Too Large"**

# Resolving HTTP 413 "Request Entity Too Large"

# Issue Description

Users are encountering an **HTTP 413 (Request Entity Too Large)** error when attempting to upload large files to the Deploy server. This issue typically occurs during the following actions:

* Uploading large artifacts to components.  
* Uploading plugins to the Deployment automation system.  
* Managing Java Packages (e.g., uploading Java binaries via the web UI).

**Error Log:**

*java.lang.Exception: Request error: 413: \<html\>*  
*\<head\>\<title\>413 Request Entity Too Large\</title\>\</head\>*  
*\<body\>*  
*\<center\>\<h1\>413 Request Entity Too Large\</h1\>\</center\>*  
*\<hr\>\<center\>nginx\</center\>*  
*\</body\>*  
*\</html\>*

When uploading Java as part of “Manage Java Packages” on the Deploy server through Chrome  
Error:  
*\<html\> \<head\>\<title\>413 Request Entity Too Large\</title\>\</head\> \<body\> \<center\>\<h1\>413 Request Entity Too Large\</h1\>\</center\> \<hr\>\<center\>nginx\</center\> \</body\> \</html\> \<\!-- a padding to disable MSIE and Chrome friendly error page \--\> \<\!-- a padding to disable MSIE and Chrome friendly error page \--\> \<\!-- a padding to disable MSIE and Chrome friendly error page \--\> \<\!-- a padding to disable MSIE and Chrome friendly error page \--\> \<\!-- a padding to disable MSIE and Chrome friendly error page \--\> \<\!-- a padding to disable MSIE and Chrome friendly error page →*

### **Root Cause:**

### The error is caused by the NGINX Ingress Controller's default configuration. The default Client Max Body Size is often restricted. When an uploaded file exceeds this limit, NGINX blocks the request before it reaches the backend service.

### **Resolution**

To resolve this, you must increase the allowed “proxy-body-size” (and optionally the “proxy-body-size”) in the Ingress annotations for the affected environment.

      **Identify the Target Ingress:**  
              Run the following command to confirm the Ingress resource name in the devops-loop namespace:  
                  $ kubectl get ingress \-n devops-loop

     **Target Ingresses:**

* **IBM Environment:** devops-loop-ibm-devops-loop-ingress  
* **HCL Environment:** devops-loop-hcl-devops-loop-ingress

####  **Update Annotations**

You need to edit the Ingress resource and add/update the following annotations. Set the values according to your maximum expected file size (e.g., 100m, 500m, 1g).

**Required Annotation:**

* nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: Controls the maximum allowed size of the client request body (the file upload).

**Optional/Related Annotation:**

* nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffer-size: Controls the buffer size for reading the response header (update if you also see 502 errors or have large headers).

**From:**   
![][image156]

To:

Please add a new entry for “nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size” if it is not already present.  
![][image157]

      

# **Configure Emissary Ingress Ports**

# Configure Emissary Ingress Ports (Optional, if ports are not configured during the Loop installation)

To allow agents to connect via WebSocket (WSS) or SSH, the Emissary Ingress must have specific ports exposed.

1. Agent Connection URL Construction as below  
* **Format:** `wss://<HOST_IP>.nip.io:7919`  
* **Example:** `wss://10.190.116.49.nip.io:7919`  
    
2. Verify Existing Emissary Ports  
   Check the currently exposed ports on the Emissary service.  
        $ kubectl get services \-n emissary  
     
3. Patch Emissary Ports (If Missing)  
   If the ports 7919 (Deploy Agent), 7920 (Build Agent), or 9022 (Console/SSH) are missing from the output above, run the following patch command to open them:

   kubectl patch svc emissary-ingress \-n emissary \--type='json' \-p='\[  
     {"op": "add", "path": "/spec/ports/-", "value": {"name":"deploy-wss","port":7919,"targetPort":7919,"protocol":"TCP"}},  
     {"op": "add", "path": "/spec/ports/-", "value": {"name":"build-wss","port":7920,"targetPort":7920,"protocol":"TCP"}},  
     {"op": "add", "path": "/spec/ports/-", "value": {"name":"control-ssh","port":9022,"targetPort":9022,"protocol":"TCP"}}  
   \]'  
     
4. Final Validation  
   After patching, re-run the verification command:  
     
   **$ kubectl get services \-n emissary**  
   NAME                     TYPE           CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)                                                                   AGE  
   emissary-ingress         LoadBalancer   10.96.173.104   10.244.0.1    80:30293/TCP,443:30996/TCP**,7919**:30217/TCP,7**920**:31199/TCP,**9022**:31285/TCP   6d18h  
   emissary-ingress-admin   ClusterIP      10.96.45.210    \<none\>        8877/TCP,8005/TCP                                                         6d18h  
     
   Ensure the new ports are listed. The external agent should now be able to establish a connection to the server.

# **Add teams to the New Deploy agent**

# Add teams to the New Deploy agent:

# Issue Description**:** 

When new deploy agents are installed without specifying any Teams, non-administrator users cannot see the agent listed under **Resources \> Agents**.

**Solution 1: Add your username to the Administrator role on Teams**

1. **Grant Administrator Access:**  
   * Log in to the **Deploy UI**.  
   * Navigate to **Settings \> Security \> Teams**.  
   * Select the specific **Team Name** (e.g., Team Name with Teamspace or Loop name).  
   * Go to **Role Members \> Administrator**.  
   * Click **Add** and insert your username.  
2. **Add the Required Team to the Agent:**  
   * Log in to the **Deploy UI**.  
   * Navigate to **Resources \> Agents \> \[Agent\_Name\]**.  
   * Go to **Configuration \> Basic Settings \> Teams**.  
   * Click **Add Teams** and select the appropriate team.  
   * Click **Save**.

**Solution 2: Configure Teams during Agent Installation**

When installing the agent, you can specify the teams immediately to ensure visibility and access.

* **Prompt:** "Enter teams (and types) to add this agent to, separated by commas."  
  **Enter teams (and types) to add this agent to, separated by commas.**  
  The default value is None.  
  Agents can be added to teams the first time they connect to the server. The agent is assigned to the specific teams the first time that it connects to the server. Separate multiple teams by commas. Trailing spaces are ignored. Team names that do not exist are also ignored. To specify the agent's security type for a team, provide the team and security type in the following format: team:type.

**Overview**

This involves exposing the Kubernetes service via a LoadBalancer with a static External IP and ensuring the necessary communication ports are open on the Emissary ingress.

# Add External IP

1. **Determine your Kubernetes Host IP:** Use ifconfig (Linux/Mac) or ipconfig (Windows) to find the IP address of your Kubernetes host node. (Example used below: 10.190.116.49).  
2. **Identify the Kubernetes Service:** List the services to confirm the correct service name.  
*  Run \`kubectl get svc\` to list services.  
*  Identify the \`devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod\` or ‘**devops-loop-hcl-launch-server-prod’**  service.

     Note:

  IBM Service: **devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod**

  HCL Service: **devops-loop-hcl-launch-server-prod**


3.  Edit the Service Type:   
*      Edit the service using \`kubectl edit svc devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod\`.  
*      Change the service type from \`type: ClusterIP\` to \`type: LoadBalancer\`


4. Patching the Service to add External IP:  
   Run the patch command to append the externalIPs field to the service specification. Replace the IP address below with your actual Host IP.

                  $ **kubectl patch service devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod \-p '{"spec": {"externalIPs": \["10.190.116.49"\]}}'**

   

5. Verification: Confirm that the External IP and TYPE have been successfully applied.

   $ **kubectl get svc devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod \-o wide**

   NAME                       TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP     PORT(S)                         AGE   SELECTOR

   devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod   **LoadBalancer**   10.96.96.160   **10.190.116.49**   8080:30635/TCP,7919:31531/TCP   42d   [app.kubernetes.io/component=srv,app.kubernetes.io/instance=devops-loop,app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-ucd-prod](http://app.kubernetes.io/component=srv,app.kubernetes.io/instance=devops-loop,app.kubernetes.io/name=ibm-ucd-prod)

6. **Expected Output:** The EXTERNAL-IP column should now display your host IP (e.g., 10.190.116.49) instead of \<none\>. You can now connect your external DB client using this IP and Port 3306\.

**Overview** This document outlines the procedures for retrieving database credentials, connecting to the MySQL database within the Kubernetes cluster, and optionally exposing the service for external access (e.g., for use with clients like DbVisualizer).

1. # Access the Deploy server pod {#access-the-deploy-server-pod}

1.  **Identify the Deploy server pod:**

     $ kubectl get pods

   

2.  **Deploy server installation path:**

    $ kubectl exec \-it devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod-0 \-- /bin/bash

       bash-5.1$ cd opt/ibm-ucd/server/

   

3. **DevOps deploy uses MySQL Database**

   From Deploy's installed properties

   

   hibernate.connection.url=jdbc\\:mysql\\://devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod-mysql.devops-loop.svc.cluster.local\\:3306/ucdtest

   hibernate.connection.username=ucduser

   agentcomm.uri=wss\\://devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod-0.devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod-hl\\:7919

   server.external.web.url=https\\://[10.190.116.49.nip.io/deploy](http://10.190.116.49.nip.io/deploy)

   

4.  **In secured-installed.properties**

   hibernate.connection.password=pbe{xxxxx}

2. # Retrieve Database Credentials {#retrieve-database-credentials}

   

1. **Run the command below to find the secrets name**

      $ kubectl get secrets \-n devops-loop | grep \-i secret

   devops-loop-build-secrets                               Opaque                           3      42d

   devops-loop-control-ini-secrets                         Opaque                           1      42d

   devops-loop-ibm-devopsplan-prod-db-secret               Opaque                           3      42d

   **devops-loop-secrets**                                     Opaque                           3      42d

   devops-loop-tls-secret                                  kubernetes.io/tls                3      42d

   jwt-secret                                              Opaque                           1      42d

   mongodb-url-secret                                      Opaque                           1      42d

   

2. Get “dbpassword” from command “kubectl get secret devops-loop-secrets \-o yaml”  
3. Run the command “ echo \<Value from Step 2\>| base64 \--decode”  
4.  Run the following command to extract the dbpassword key and decode it from Base64. You can combine (step 2 and 3\) by command   
                         $ **kubectl get secret devops-loop-secrets \-o jsonpath="{.data.dbpassword}" | base64 \--decode**

# 3\. Steps to connect to the Database of Deploy {#3.-steps-to-connect-to-the-database-of-deploy}

                  $ kubectl get pod | grep mysql

      $ kubectl exec \-it devops-loop-ibm-ucd-prod-mysql-74bf4d76cf-k9lgq \-- mysql \-u ucduser \-p

# Database Connection and Management Guide for DevOps Velocity

**Table of Contents:**

[1\. Retrieve Database Credentials](#retrieve-database-credentials-1)

[2\. Connect to the Velocity Database](#2.-connect-to-the-velocity-database)

> > > [2.1. Method A: Interactive Step-by-Step](#2.1.-method-a:-interactive-step-by-step)

> > > [2.2. Method B: Single-Line Connection](#2.2.-method-b:-single-line-connection)

[3\. Add an External IP to the MongoDB Service (Optional)](#3.-add-an-external-ip-to-the-mongodb-service-\(optional\))

**Overview** This document outlines the procedures for retrieving the root password, connecting to the MongoDB database within the Kubernetes cluster, and optionally exposing the service for external access (e.g., for use with clients like MongoDB Compass).

1. # Retrieve Database Credentials {#retrieve-database-credentials-1}

   1.  **Identify the Mongo DB secret:**  
        $  kubectl get secrets \-n devops-loop  
        
   2. Get the password  
      Run the following command to extract the mongodb-root-password and decode it from Base64:  
      

               $ kubectl get secret devops-loop-mongo-mongodb \-o jsonpath="{.data.mongodb-root-password}" | base64 \--decode  
     
   3. Construct the Connection String  
         Use the decoded password to format your connection string as follows:  
* **Syntax:** mongodb://root:\<PASSWORD\>@\<HOST\_IP\>:27017/  
* **Example:** mongodb://root:cACVFSXxxiS@10.190.116.49.nip.io:27017/


# 2\. Connect to the Velocity Database {#2.-connect-to-the-velocity-database}

You can connect to the MongoDB instance by executing the Mongo Shell (`mongosh`) directly inside the Kubernetes pod.

##           2.1. Method A: Interactive Step-by-Step {#2.1.-method-a:-interactive-step-by-step}

1. Find the MongoDB Pod:

     $ kubectl get pod | grep mongodb

2. Enter the Pod shell  
                             $ kubectl exec \-it devops-loop-mongo-mongodb-74cc576d96-5hm6l \-- /bin/bash  
     
3. Run the Mongo Shell inside the pod:

    $ mongosh "mongodb://10.190.116.49.nip.io:27017" \--username root \-p cACVFSXxxiS

   

   ##   2.2. **Method B: Single-Line Connection** {#2.2.-method-b:-single-line-connection}

1. **Execute the Connection Command:** Replace \<POD\_NAME\>, \<HOST\_IP\>, and \<PASSWORD\> with your specific values.**Syntax:** kubectl exec \-it \<POD\_NAME\> \-- mongosh "mongodb://\<HOST\_IP\>:27017" \--username root \-p \<PASSWORD\>

               

                  $ **kubectl exec \-it devops-loop-mongo-mongodb-74cc576d96-5hm6l \-- mongosh "mongodb://10.190.116.49.nip.io:27017" \--username root \-p cACVFSXxxiS**

# Configure MCP

# Pre-Requisite:

### **What you actually need to install Copilot:**

* **A GitHub Account:** You must have a standard GitHub account.  
* **An Active Subscription:** You need a subscription (Copilot Free, Pro, Business, or Enterprise).  
  You can check your subscription on  [https://github.com/settings/billing/licensing](https://github.com/settings/billing/licensing)  
  ![][image158]

### **How to get started right now:**

1. Open VS Code.  
2. Press `Ctrl+Shift+X` (Extensions view).  
3. **The Extensions:** Search for **GitHub Copilot** and click **Install**. You simply install the **GitHub Copilot** extension from the VS Code Marketplace. It will automatically include **GitHub Copilot Chat**.  
4. Click the **“Sign in to use AI Features”** on bottom right and sign in with your GitHub account

You must have completed the following tasks:

1. Ensured that you have installed VS Code and the GitHub Copilot extension.  
   ![][image159]  
2. Obtained the MCP Server URL. For example: [https://hostname/loop/mcp](https://hostname/loop/mcp)  
3. Close the VS Code

## Open Powershell

1. Run the following command to Set `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED` to `'0. This` tells Node.js to **ignore all SSL certificate errors**.  
        Command  
         \>  $env:NODE\_TLS\_REJECT\_UNAUTHORIZED='0'

           

2. To Open VS Code, run the command below   
         \>  code

3. Create an empty directory on your local system. Example “loop20”  
4. On VS Code \> File \> “Add Folder to workspace” and select folder “loop20”.  
4. Create a new folder named .vscode inside that directory, if not present.  
5. Create a file named mcp.json inside the .vscode folder.  
6. In the Bottom text editor **Add Server**.  
7. Choose **HTTP** as the server type, when prompted for the transport type.  
   The DevOps Loop MCP Server uses HTTP-based transport.  
8. Enter the **MCP Server URL**, in the **URL** field. For example: [https://10.190.116.49.nip.io/loop/mcp](https://hostname/loop/mcp)  
   VS Code automatically generates the required mcp.json configuration.  
9. Enter a name for the server. For example: “**Loop MCP Server”**.

   Sometimes you have to follow step 10, 11, 12 (Optional)  
10. *Select **Workspace**, when VS Code prompts you to choose where to save this configuration.*  
    1. ***Global** – used for all VS Code workspaces*  
       2. ***Workspace** – used only in the current folder/project*  
       3. ***Note:** Selecting Workspace automatically creates a .vscode folder and generates a mcp.json file inside it.*  
11. *Click the Extensions icon ![][image160] and navigate to **MCP-servers installed**.*  
12. *Click the Settings icon ![][image161] next to Loop MCP server.*

13. Select the **Start server** option.  
    VS Code displays a notification stating that the MCP server requires authentication.  
14. Click **Allow** to proceed.  
    A second notification is displayed asking whether you want to open an external website.  
15. Click **Open**.  
    Your default browser opens and displays the DevOps Loop login page.  
16. Sign in with your DevOps Loop credentials.  
    A consent screen is displayed requesting access to MCP tools, loop APIs, and basic profile information.  
17. Click **Yes** to approve and complete the connection.  
    ![][image162]

    After successful authentication, VS Code displays the list of available MCP tools. See [MCP tools available in DevOps Loop](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/SSGB5S_2.0.0/docs/topics/c_mcp_server_integration.html#c_mcp_server_integration__section_ykz_h22_nhc).  
18. On VS code \> chat (Right corner) \> Configuration tools \> MCP server name (Example: **Loop MCP Server)**  
19. Test with your query “list all Teamspaces” on copilot chat  
    ![][image163]

Troubleshooting:

List the user on my Teamspace

You need to set up GitHub Copilot and be signed in to use Chat.

# Configure OIDC for Authentication

Configure OIDC for Authentication

This document describes the steps to follow to configure OIDC as the authentication provider for DevOps Loop. Follow the instructions below to configure

* Login to keycloak using the URL https://\<login\_URL\>/auth/ , example [https://10.190.116.48.nip.io/auth/](https://10.190.116.48.nip.io/auth/)  
    
  *Default user ID for keycloak is : “keycloak”*  
  *Default password is: “66e91c191d4dd0e622a2ca9a3d06d62dba69a90179919c9446a854a860ae65f7”*

* Once logged in go to “Manage realms” and select ***devops-automation*** realm  
    
  ![][image167]  
    
* Go to Identity providers on the left hand side pane . It will list out all the Identity providers options that can be integrated with Loop. In this example we will be using OpenID connect v1  
    
  ![][image168]  
    
* We then move to configuring the OIDC . In this example we have already created an okta application at the Okta end. The alias name could be anything that you would like to configure by default it is ***oidc***  
    
  ![][image169]  
  Note as you change the alias name the Redirect URI will change. So the redirect URI is https://10.190.116.48.nip.io/auth/realms/devops-automation/broker/\<alias name\>/endpoint  
    
  This redirect URI should be used for configuring the application at the OKTA end. In this example we are sticking with the default oidc so our redirect URI is [https://10.190.116.48.nip.io/auth/realms/devops-automation/broker/oidc/endpoint](https://10.190.116.48.nip.io/auth/realms/devops-automation/broker/oidc/endpoint)

  Once you configure the application at the Okta(identity provider) end you would get the client ID , client secret and the discovery endpoint/URL for configuration. We would need these to configure OIDC at Loop end.

* Put the discovery endpoint provided by the identity provider in the Discovery endpoint field  
    
  ![][image170]  
    
* Post that click on the Show metadata to automatically fetch all the endpoints  
    
  ![][image171]  
    
* Provide the Client ID and Client Secret and leave all the other fields as default. ![][image172]  
    
  Click on “Add” to save the configuration. The provider would be created.  
    
* Once the provider is created, click on “Advanced”   
  ![][image173]  
    
  It will list out all the other options that we can configure . We go to *Scopes* field to add the scopes that we would like to be as part of the login. In this example we are adding openid, profile, email and groups   
    
  ![][image174]  
* Now we move to adding mappers. Mappers map the values/attributes that we are pulling from Okta end to keycloak end.  
    
  Click on the *Mappers* tab and *Add mapper.* In this example we are adding “email”   
    
  ![][image175]  
  Similarly add the other mappers that you want to add.   
    
* Once the above steps are done you are ready to login using the Okta. Open the login page and we should see the option to login using Okta that we configured  
    
  ![][image176]  
    
* Post login , you would see the new user under the “users” in keycloak  
    
  ![][image177]  
    
  By default the created user doesn’t have any  permissions. We need to give permission using Role Mapping.      

* Add the user to the groups *“Admins”* and *“Users”* . Click on the created user under “Users” \>  created user \> Groups .  Click on *Join Group*  and add the user to the Admins and the Users group.  
  ![][image178]

* Click on the created user under “Users” \>  created user \> Role Mapping. Then click on “Assign role” and assign the required roles.  
    
  ![][image179]

When you try to clone a Control repo, you might face the error like below screen:

, 

![][image184]

For this, you have to create a PAT token in CONTROL and use it as explained [here]()

# Creating PAT Token for control

**Creating PAT Token for Control**

1\) I generated an access token with name PAT1 here..

![][image185]

2\) While creating the token, select “All” and give permission for all items in it:

![][image186]

3\) As soon as you create a PAT token, you will see the Hex value for that token.  
The text will be shown only once (it will not be shown again so copy the hex string somewhere to remember it):

![][image187]

That hex string is your PAT that acts as the password when you clone the Control repository

\==============================

![][image188]

4\) Then form your URL Like this for “git clone” command:

https://\<MyUserID\>:\<PAT Hexa value we cpoid\>@\<Control Repo link\>

[https://srinivasamurthya-hcl.com:3212d98f49330f08c50eec05b85d37019eb7bb07@10.190.116.50.nip.io/control/avinashTS/loop4](https://srinivasamurthya-hcl.com:3212d98f49330f08c50eec05b85d37019eb7bb07@10.190.116.50.nip.io/control/avinashTS/loop4)

Note: You have to replace @ character in the email to “-” (hyphen)  
srinivasamurthya@hcl.com will become srinivasamurthya\-hcl.com

So the final command will be something like below:

git clone https://srinivasamurthya-hcl.com:3212d98f49330f08c50eec05b85d37019eb7bb07@10.190.116.50.nip.io/control/avinashTS/loop4

5\) So the final git clone command will run like below:  
![][image189]

6\) In some scenarios you might get SSL error when running the “git clone” command like below.  
Then we can set the below variables to skip the SSL verification:  
\============

git \-c http.sslVerify=false clone  
git config \--global http.sslVerify false  
\============
